title: Hashim Malallah
text:
Hello!
I am a Ph.D. candidate in Political Science at Florida State University. I study international conflict and cooperation, primarily within the context of MENA politics and American foreign policy. My dissertation focuses on the intersection of domestic and international politics to explain variation in third-party support for conflict actors. Methodologically, my work combines causal inference techniques for observational data, machine learning, and text-as-data methods.
My other projects examine the consequences of high-level diplomatic visits, with implications for interstate peace processes, host states’ policy concessions, recognition politics, and international oil trade.
Prior to FSU, I received my MA from New York University, and my BA from Temple University.

title: Research
text:
Working Papers
U.S. Foreign Policy and Arab Israeli Relations: A Quantitative Approach. Revise and Resubmit at International Studies Quarterly


Abstract

Why did some Arab states sign and maintain normalization agreements with Israel while others did not? Prior research focuses more on rivalry termination as indicator of rapprochement, yet it is unclear why rapprochement endures and recurs after failure despite high commitment problems. In this article, I examine the foreign policy conditions under which Arab Israeli rapprochement is likely to occur, succeeds, and recurs. Focusing on US mediation, I propose and test different mechanisms linking US diplomatic visits to Arab Israeli rapprochement. US leaders share private information via face-to-face diplomacy to persuade or subsidize the normalization concession, akin to ‘information lobbying’. Diplomatic visits thus have bigger impact on Arab Israeli rapprochement when the recipient is ex ante less diplomatically embedded with the US. Using data on US diplomatic visits for the sample of MENA countries from 1950 to 2022, I find support to the theoretical prediction: exchanged visits between US and Arab leaders increase the likelihood of normalization onset and success. US Presidential visits have bigger impact on normalization onset when alternative channels of diplomatic communication are weak or have been disrupted. These findings highlight the role of in-person diplomacy situated within the broader diplomatic environment in shaping interstate peace processes.

When Do Visits Lead to Concessions? Alliedness and Host-State Responses to U.S. Presidential Visits. (with James Kim and Chamseul Yu) [Manuscript] Under Review


Abstract

When do U.S. presidential visits generate policy concessions from host states? Prior research has primarily focused on the downstream political consequences of high-level visits yet relatively less attention is given to the conditions under which host states reciprocate visits with concessions. We argue that the effectiveness of diplomatic visits in eliciting host-state concessions is conditional on the level of alliedness between the United States and the host state. Weakly aligned host states have stronger incentives to reciprocate because U.S. diplomatic attention is rarer and carries greater marginal value. This increases both host leaders’ willingness to give something meaningful in return and their political opportunity to justify concessions to domestic audiences. Moving beyond formal defense pacts, we introduce a novel measure of interstate alliedness using a Bayesian latent measurement approach. Using data on U.S. presidential visits from 1977 to 2020 and a panel matching with difference-in-differences (DID) design, we find empirical support for our theoretical prediction. Across economic, diplomatic, and security domains, U.S. presidential visits consistently generate greater policy concessions among weakly aligned host states than among closely aligned ones. Our findings suggest that the existing status of the bilateral relationship is an important factor in determining whether diplomatic visits generate policy returns.

Side Taking in Conflicts: The Case of the Palestine Question


Abstract

When and Why do third-party states take sides in protracted conflicts? Research on partisan interventions has largely focused on ties between third parties and conflict actors, but pays less attention to how domestic politics and great-power dependence jointly shape diplomatic support. I argue that leaders’ ideological preferences drive support for parties involved in protracted conflicts. However, the ideology induced effect is conditional on the degree to which third parties are vulnerable to great powers pressure. I test the argument on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, focusing on UN General Assembly voting records on the Question of Palestine from 1947 to 2020. Leveraging (quasi) exogenous reversals in the ideology of the chief executives across UN member states and using a panel matching with difference-in-differences design, I show that shifts to left leadership decrease vote alignment with Israel, while reversals from left to non-left leadership increase vote alignment with Israel. Yet the ideology induced effect is muted among states that are highly dependent on US economic support, particularly in the post-Cold War era. I also show that left leaders are generally less likely to abstain on Palestine-related resolutions, but economically dependent left governments increasingly turn to abstention in the long run as a strategy to reconcile competing domestic and international incentives. The findings speaks to broad literatures on side taking in conflicts and the domestic politics of foreign policy, by highlighting the role and limits of domestic ideological preferences and hierarchical relations with major powers in shaping when, why, and how third parties express diplomatic support in protracted conflicts.

Teaching Evaluations


Selected Student Evaluations

• The instructor is so passionate about the topics in this class that I was truly excited to come to class and listen to his lectures.
• Really enjoyed this class. Such a nice professor and I learned so much. He really knew how to engage the class and taught very well. I like how engaged he was with students.
• I really enjoyed his passion for teaching and connecting with each student. His class never felt like a burden to attend, mostly because he was always in a positive mood and kept me interested and engaged. He mixed in Kahoots and group discussions which made the class a lot more fun.
• The collaborative environment that Hashim created in the classroom was great, and I was able to learn a lot from him and from my peers. His lectures were also very informative and interesting.
• I loved this course with Professor Malallah! I would definitely recommend it to other students.
• Overall, I think he is an excellent teacher and has been my favorite teacher at FSU. I don’t know if I can think of any suggestions because I truly enjoyed his class.
• He genuinely cares about the students and is extremely passionate about his work.
• I really hope he keeps teaching. He told us that he has always had a passion for teaching and that we were his first ever in-person class. I want to say thank you for this class, it really made me feel confident in my choice of major and what I want to do for my career. Mr. Malallah’s passion for the subject combined with him being an amazing human being made this class such an enjoyable experience for me.
• I really enjoyed his lectures and learned a lot. I like the amount of discussion and the surveys due before class really got you thinking about the lecture material before class.
• The way Professor Malallah connects with students is crucial to it being an engaging class. He also does a good job encouraging students to speak and incorporating fun/innovate experiences.
• He made the class engaging, not just lecture-based, which really helped.
• I appreciate your passion for teaching and your efforts to engage students. Your speaker notes are especially helpful during review sessions and when it’s hard to understand what is being said.
• He is very hands on and I like that he makes us engage in discussion to help test our own knowledge of the subjects. I also think his lectures were very helpful.
• Hashim made the course very engaging by using video clips, real world examples, and discussions. These discussions were a great tool because they allowed us to apply the content and think critically, and get a break from lecturing to engage with our peers.
• he was a very fun professor. he makes it clear that he has much to improve on and takes criticism seriously.
• Overall, I really enjoyed this class and it was very interactive and fun. Hashim is very easy to talk to about grades and assignments and very helpful with everything.
• I enjoy the class is a mix of presenting and discussion. I think it is important to learn our peers persepctives. Also, the fact that this class is continuously updated based on daily events is important as there are many topics to discuss.
• I love how knowledgable he is and how he asks class/group questions to engage the subject (we can learn from each other) . I also enjoy how he keeps us up to date with each current issue as well as other ones in the past. Great teacher
• I really like how he encourages discussion and will come sit with the groups. I really appreciate the level of engagement he provides for the class.
• I really enjoyed how he would always ask the class questions about what we learned in class and made the class very interactive and fun. He also would ask us about sports and weekend plans we had to make use feel more comfortable and involved.
• The projects required use of knowledge of the class and other international relations knowledge which allowed me to practice my skills, and taught me valuable lessons about IR.
